facts.fact: pH measures hydrogen ion concentration on a 0–14 scale, where 7.0 is neutral.
The pH scale is logarithmic, so each one-unit step is a tenfold change in acidity.
KH (carbonate hardness) measures carbonates and bicarbonates. It buffers the water against sudden pH changes.
GH (general hardness) measures calcium and magnesium. These minerals matter for fish bones and muscles, shrimp molting, snail shells and plant growth.
1 dKH equals 17.9 ppm.
Most freshwater fish do well at pH 6.5–8.0. Typical KH is 4–8 dKH (70–140 ppm) and typical GH is 4–8 dGH (70–140 ppm).
Discus and Caridina crystal shrimp suit 0–3 dKH (0–50 ppm) and about 3 dGH (50 ppm) or less. African cichlids suit more than 10 dKH (above 180 ppm).
Livebearers, goldfish and African cichlids prefer higher GH.
A WSAVA vet proceedings paper gives an ideal alkalinity of 100–250 mg/L and an ideal hardness of 100–250 mg/L for most freshwater fish. Discus prefer softer water and African cichlids harder water.
Natural freshwater ranges from slightly below pH 6.0 to about 8.5. Most freshwater fish adapt to gradual change within that range, but rapid pH changes harm them.
High hardness usually comes with high alkalinity and high pH.
Below pH 6.5, most ammonia exists as the nontoxic ammonium ion. Above 6.5, accumulated ammonia can quickly become toxic, and higher temperature raises its toxicity further.
Below pH 6.5, nitrifying bacteria slow down. Above 7.5, more free ammonia forms, which is very toxic to shrimp.
Recommended GH for shrimp: Caridina 3–4, Neocaridina 4–8, Sulawesi 6–8.
Recommended TDS for shrimp: Caridina about 80–120 ppm, Neocaridina about 180–250 ppm, Sulawesi about 200 ppm.
Recommended KH by tank type: community 3–8 dKH, planted CO2 tanks 2–5 dKH, Caridina tanks on active substrate 0–1 dKH, African cichlid tanks 8–15 dKH.
This source puts the pH most freshwater fish live well in at about 5.5–7.5. If pH sits at 7.5–8 and is stable, it says no adjustment is needed.
Fish in a pH crash may swim frantically, become lethargic or breathe rapidly.
Signs of low GH: poor appetite, slow growth, lethargy, faded color, mineral deficiency in plants, molting trouble in shrimp, and thin or pitted snail shells.
pH crash signs: gasping at the surface and erratic swimming; faded color, clamped fins and appetite loss; in critical cases, lying on the bottom, excess mucus and sudden deaths.
Caridina shrimp such as Crystal Red and Taiwan Bee often die before fish show distress, so dead shrimp are an early warning of a pH crash.
A pH reading below 6.0 confirms a crash.
Large pH swings usually mean KH is too low to buffer the water.
Biological filtration consumes carbonates, so alkalinity falls over time. Low alkalinity can cause sudden, deadly pH shifts.
At about 0–1 dKH the water has no buffer left. Nitrification, CO2 injection, active substrates and organic acids all use up KH.
A CO2 overdose, for example from a stuck solenoid or a cylinder dumping at end of tank, can drop pH from 6.8 to below 5.5 within an hour.
Active substrates (aquasoil) usually stop buffering after 12–24 months.
Some substrates change pH, so the effect of a substrate should be checked before using it.
In a pH crash, turn off CO2 and increase surface agitation and aeration.
Do a 20–30% water change with dechlorinated water, not 50% or more at once, and let pH rise no faster than about 0.3–0.5 units per hour.
If pH is still low, test hourly and do 15–20% water changes about an hour apart. Aim for recovery over roughly 4–8 hours.
Emergency KH dose: about 1 teaspoon (roughly 5 g) of baking soda per 100 L, dissolved in tank water and added slowly. It raises KH by about 2–3 dKH. Do not add more than this at once.
Commercial KH buffers include Seachem Alkaline Buffer and SL Aqua KH Builder. Add gradually and test after each dose.
Crushed coral raises pH, KH and GH. Use about 1 lb per 10 gallons in the substrate, or put it in a filter bag. Replace every 6–12 months.
At pH 8.0, crushed coral raises KH while pH changes less. At lower pH, it raises both pH and KH.
Calcium carbonate raises both GH and KH. To raise GH alone, add calcium and magnesium salts that contain no carbonates or bicarbonates.
Wonder Shells or Seachem Equilibrium can also raise hardness.
To lower pH, KH and GH, do fewer water changes so the tank acidifies, or mix in RO/DI water gradually.
To fix low alkalinity, add carbonates or do water changes with higher-alkalinity water.
CO2 injection lowers pH without changing KH.
Crushed dolomite or coral in the substrate raises pH by releasing calcium carbonate.
pH-down chemicals do not last because KH pulls pH back. Package doses are only accurate with RO water. The lasting fix is to lower KH with a different water source or RO water.
RO water removes about 90–99% of impurities and has a pH near 7. Minerals must be added back to suit the species.
For shrimp, use RO/DI water and add a calcium-and-magnesium-only remineralizer. Example from one farm: 9 ml of Nutrafin shrimp minerals in a 50 L tank gives about 100 ppm TDS.
Driftwood releases tannins that lower pH and tint the water brown. This tint does not harm fish or plants.
1) Test pH, KH and GH, and look up what each species needs.
2) Find and remove whatever is pushing pH off target before you adjust it.
3) Correct KH first. To lower pH lastingly, reduce KH. To stabilize pH, raise KH.
4) Change values slowly, then retest after each water change or dose. Keep a log to track trends.
Do partial water changes of about 25% with dechlorinated water, weekly in new tanks and 1–2 times a month in established ones.
Test KH monthly, or every two weeks if you run CO2 or active substrate. Act when KH trends down, before it reaches zero.
In CO2 and planted tanks, keep KH above roughly 2–3 dKH. Replace active substrate at around 12–24 months.
Do not let KH fall to 2 dKH or below, because pH swings become dangerous.
Where tap water is already hard, extra water changes may be enough to keep hardness up.
Assuming pH must be held perfectly constant. Some daily fluctuation is normal; sudden spikes are the real danger.
Assuming high GH means enough calcium. The water may be high in magnesium and low in calcium, so test calcium separately if symptoms persist.
Changing pH suddenly or doing one very large water change.
Dosing pH chemicals by guesswork without retesting, and trusting litmus paper or cheap, uncalibrated pH pens. This source says liquid test reagents are more accurate.
Boiling leaves before use reduces their effect. Soak them for a few days instead, and take carbon out of the filter.
Vietnamese keepers lower pH with dried leaves: Indian almond (lá bàng), banana, guava, mango and longan leaves, at about 1 leaf per 30 L.
Almond leaves can bring pH down to about 6.0 if enough are used. A leaf can take about 2 months to break down unless shrimp eat it.
Without an RO unit, one farm suggests 20 L purified-water jugs or 5 L bottled spring water. Do not use mineral water, and always measure TDS first.
Local shrimp keepers commonly use a TDS pen (for example Xiaomi) to track mineral levels.
Flowerhorn (cá két) and other cichlids (cá ali) like high pH, while Amazon blackwater fish like low pH.
A Vietnamese article says fish waste can raise pH. A reviewer of that article notes that waste and organic decay normally lower pH.
Water tests come as strips, dry tablets, liquid reagent kits, electronic meters and spectrophotometers. Spectrophotometers are more accurate.
Multi-test strips can measure pH, KH and GH together. Test during maintenance, when breeding or when troubleshooting.
